newsitem.title: USA: Hashimoto, Clinton urge progress on trade disputes.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto, Clinton urge progress on trade disputes.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and U.S. President Bill Clinton met briefly on Tuesday, saying their nations should solve insurance and aviation disputes without letting them disturb bilateral ties.

Most of their 30-minute chat on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly was devoted to security and global issues, a Japanese official told reporters. But with both men in the midst of re-election campaigns, their discussion also raised long-simmering trade disputes, without going into details and without the acrimony of last year's dispute over automobiles.

Clinton, who raised the issues of aviation and insurance, called for mutual efforts to break a deadlock on U.S. freight carriers' access to Japan's airports and the ability of U.S. insurers to operate in primary Japanese sectors, the Japanese official said.
Hashimoto told Clinton he agreed the two countries should seek accomodation but added that sectoral trade disputes should not threaten bilateral ties, the official said.
Hashimoto was trade minister last year when the two economic powers struggled over trade issues involving cars and car parts, forging an 11th-hour deal that averted a trade war.
The two leaders stressed their mutual commitment to addressing grievances on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa about the heavy concentration of U.S. military bases there, the official said.

Japan, with U.S. support, has made a breakthrough in meeting Okinawan demands that the U.S. presence be reduced and intrusive military training activities be relocated to less populous areas, Hashimoto was quoted as telling Clinton.

The two leaders discussed plans to relocate and trim some Okinawa bases -- the task of a bilateral project team launched in Washington last week -- but agreed that U.S. military readiness should not be affected, the official said.

Okinawa, reluctant host to about 75 percent of the U.S. facilties in Japan and half of the 47,000 U.S. troops stationed there, exploded in anger last year after the rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.

Clinton expressed concern about recent turmoil in Korea after commandos from a North Korean submarine were caught in South Korea and said Washington would continue to spearhead efforts to stem Pyongyang's suspected nuclear weapons ambitions under a 1994 accord, the official said.

Hashimoto followed his talks with Clinton with a speech to the Council on Foreign Relations in which he underscored his plans to deregulate Japan's economy. "The basic principle is to make deregulation the norm," Hashimoto said.
